concepts.mechanism_summary: Suppletion is a form of morphological irregularity whereby a change in a grammatical category triggers a change in word form, with a different (suppletive) root substituting for the normal one. It arises from competition of Vocabulary items for insertion into a terminal node, where a more highly specified item wins. Suppletive forms are overwhelmingly restricted to the most frequently used lexical items and persist due to high token frequency.

atoms.verbatim_quote: a change in a grammatical category triggers a change in word form, with a different (suppletive) root substituting for the normal one
atoms.mechanism_atom: A grammatical feature change causes an entirely different root to substitute for the expected one (e.g., go -> went), driven by lexical competition at terminal node insertion

atoms.verbatim_quote: Suppletion arises from the competition of Vocabulary items for insertion into a terminal node
atoms.mechanism_atom: Morphosyntactic feature bundles at a terminal node induce competition among lexical entries, with the most specified vocabulary item winning insertion, irrespective of root identity

atoms.verbatim_quote: a morphological system will tend to retain irregular forms only if they are 'sufficiently frequent'
atoms.mechanism_atom: High token frequency retains suppletive irregularity across generations; low-frequency paradigms regularize under analogical pressure

source_results.title: Mechanisms of tone sandhi rule application

concepts.mechanism_summary: Sandhi is a phonological phenomenon in which sounds of morphemes or words undergo modification at or near their boundaries due to the influence of adjacent sounds. The process encompasses assimilation, deletion, insertion, and vowel harmony at morpheme/word junctions. Tone sandhi specifically involves rightward spreading (a tone from a preceding syllable extending its influence to the following one) or contour simplification (intricate tone contours reduced to simpler forms to facilitate articulation).

atoms.verbatim_quote: rightward spreading, in which a tone from a preceding syllable extends its influence to the following one
atoms.mechanism_atom: A tonal feature propagates rightward from a source syllable to adjacent target syllables, overwriting or modifying their underlying tonal specification

atoms.verbatim_quote: contour simplification, where intricate tone contours are reduced to simpler forms to facilitate articulation and perception
atoms.mechanism_atom: Complex tonal contours alternate to simplified level tones at domain boundaries, driven by articulatory and perceptual economy

concepts.mechanism_summary: Reduplication is a morphological process in which the root or stem (or part thereof) is repeated exactly or with a slight change, with the copied element (the reduplicant) attached to the base. It operates at the interface between phonology and morphology as a non-linear/non-concatenative process. The function encodes concepts such as plurality, repetition, intensity, or continuance through copying.

atoms.mechanism_atom: A morphological operation copies all or part of a base form and attaches the copy as a prefix, suffix, or infix to express grammatical or semantic distinctions

atoms.mechanism_atom: The copy-attach operation produces iconic/symbolic meaning shifts (intensity, plurality, continuance) directly from structural repetition of form

concepts.mechanism_summary: Diglossia is a sociolinguistic situation in which two varieties of the same language coexist in a speech community, each assigned to distinct social domains: a high (H) variety for formal, governmental, and written contexts and a low (L) variety for informal, spoken, everyday interaction. At the social level, each variety is the only socially acceptable form in its assigned sphere, so speakers switch systematically between H and L based on domain, interlocutor, and register. Charles Ferguson introduced the English term in 1959.

atoms.verbatim_quote: each of the two dialects has certain spheres of social interaction assigned to it and in the assigned spheres it is the only socially acceptable dialect
atoms.mechanism_atom: Social norms separate a community's linguistic repertoire into domain-stratified varieties (H/L), with rigid domain boundaries determining which variety is deployed

atoms.verbatim_quote: diglossia is a social situation concerning a society in which there are two languages related in such a way that they have different social functions
atoms.mechanism_atom: Speakers alternate between H and L varieties as a function of situational domain (formal/informal), producing systematic register-conditioned switching across contexts

source_results.title: Liminality Definition for Intro to Anthropology | Fiveable

concepts.mechanism_summary: Liminality is the quality of ambiguity occurring in the middle stage of a rite of passage, when participants no longer hold their pre-ritual status but have not yet attained the status they will hold when the rite is complete. During this liminal phase, participants stand at the threshold between prior and new identity structures; their normal social roles are dissolved, and they experience disorientation and potential transformation. Turner identified communitas — a bond of egalitarian solidarity — as a characteristic emergent property of liminal collectivity.

atoms.mechanism_atom: Shared liminal experience produces communitas — an egalitarian solidarity state that emerges when hierarchical distinctions are suspended among co-participants

source_results.title: Cargo cults | Open Encyclopedia of Anthropology

concepts.mechanism_summary: Cargo cults are Melanesian social movements in which indigenous communities imitated the observable behaviors and symbols associated with technologically advanced societies (building runways, carving wooden headphones, performing military drills) in hope that ancestral spirits or powerful beings would deliver material goods ('cargo'). The mechanism is a disconnect between surface ritual form and underlying causal mechanism: practitioners replicate the visible surface features of an outcome-producing process without access to the causal infrastructure that actually produces outcomes. Anthropologists emphasize the movement's function as political resistance and meaning-making under colonial disruption.

atoms.verbatim_quote: indigenous society imitate the behaviors, rituals, and symbols associated with technologically advanced societies, particularly their modes of transportation and material wealth, in seemingly hope of attaining the same benefits

atoms.verbatim_quote: performing imitative rituals that are conducted without understanding the underlying cause of a phenomenon
